title: Can we predict long-duration running power output? A matter of selecting the appropriate predicting trials and empirical model
authors: Ruiz-Alias SA, Nancupil-Andrade AA, Perez-Castilla A, Garcia-Pinillos F
population: Fifteen highly trained athletes performing nine time trials (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 20, 30 and 60 min) in randomised order over 5 weeks
findings: Critical power models (work-time, power-1/time, 2- and 3-parameter hyperbolic), the Stryd and Golden Cheetah CP models, the power law and the Peronnet model were extrapolated to 60-min power and compared with actual performance.

Shortest valid configurations: CPwork and CP1/time 3-30 min (bias 8.3 W); Stryd CP 10-30 min (bias 4.2 W); CP2hyp, CP3hyp and Golden Cheetah CP 3-5-30 min (bias <5.7 W); power law 1-3-10 min (bias -1.0 W); Peronnet 4-20 min (bias -3.0 W).
All models gave valid estimates only when the predicting trials suited each model's fitting needs.
limitations: n = 15 highly trained athletes; power-meter data; 60-min ceiling, so no marathon or ultra durations; controlled trials rather than real-world logs.
implications: Choose the model according to the available efforts: CP needs efforts spread from about 3 to 30 min; the power law works with 1-3-10 min; refuse a CP fit when only very short efforts exist.
The study validates extrapolation only to 60 min; extending any of these models to marathon/ultra durations needs a durability term (not tested here).
With only short efforts logged, prefer the power law or Peronnet over CP.

verification.notes: Crossref and Europe PMC re-fetched; bias values match. Removed the researcher's claim that short-trial CP overestimates, which the abstract does not state. The 60-min cap is stated as a study limit, not a finding.
